reasoning: Decomposed into 76 verifiable statement(s). Completeness check passed. Grouped into 11 reasoning segment(s).

statements: The chief complaint is progressive dyspnea over 2 months.
The chief complaint is wheezing over 2 months.
The patient has had scant hemoptysis for 4 weeks.
The patient is 4 years after bilateral lung transplantation.
The patient’s own major concern is worsening airway symptoms.
Imaging localizes the problem to a focal obstructing lesion in the left mainstem bronchus.
The salient positive findings strongly suggest a focal endobronchial process rather than diffuse parenchymal disease alone.
She is chronically immunosuppressed with tacrolimus after lung transplant.
She is chronically immunosuppressed with prednisone after lung transplant.
She has diabetes.
She has profound chronic pancytopenia.
She has severe leukopenia.
Her white blood cell count is 0.9×10^3/mL.
These conditions increase the risk for opportunistic infection and malignancy.
Her symptoms include progressive dyspnea.
Her symptoms include focal wheezing over the left lung.
Her symptoms include scant blood-tinged sputum.
Her symptoms include 6 months of nightly sweats.
CT shows a 2.2 × 1.1 × 0.9 cm polypoid soft-tissue lesion arising from the roof of the left mainstem bronchus at the anastomotic site.
The lesion causes severe narrowing to 3 mm.
CT shows tree-in-bud nodularity in the left lower lobe.
Tree-in-bud nodularity can reflect distal endobronchial spread.
Tree-in-bud nodularity can reflect post-obstructive infectious bronchiolitis.
Bronchoscopy directly visualized a fibrinous mass protruding into the left mainstem bronchus proximal to the anastomosis.
She is afebrile.
She is oxygenating well on room air.
She denies weight loss.
CMV PCR is undetectable.
EBV PCR is undetectable.
Undetectable CMV PCR makes CMV airway disease less likely.
Undetectable EBV PCR makes EBV-driven post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder less likely.
The lesion is specifically at the bronchial anastomotic site.
The bronchial anastomotic site is an important clue favoring a transplant-related airway complication or localized infection at a structurally vulnerable site.
The focal wheeze and severe unilateral mainstem narrowing argue against simple asthma/COPD-type wheezing.
The presence of a discrete endobronchial mass argues against bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome.
Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome causes diffuse small-airway obstruction rather than a visible obstructing bronchial lesion.
The first major differential is post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.
PTLD fits because she is a transplant recipient with night sweats, hemoptysis, and an endobronchial mass.
PTLD is less favored because the lesion is centered at the anastomotic site.
PTLD is less favored because the lesion is described as fibrinous.
PTLD is less favored because there is associated tree-in-bud change suggesting airway-centered infection.
PTLD is less favored because EBV PCR is undetectable.
PTLD remains plausible.
PTLD is not the best fit.
The second differential is bronchogenic carcinoma or another endobronchial neoplasm.
Hemoptysis is compatible with bronchogenic carcinoma or another endobronchial neoplasm.
Focal wheeze is compatible with bronchogenic carcinoma or another endobronchial neoplasm.
A polypoid obstructing lesion is compatible with bronchogenic carcinoma or another endobronchial neoplasm.
The anastomotic location in an immunosuppressed lung transplant recipient makes primary malignancy less likely.
The fibrinous appearance makes primary malignancy less likely.
Distal tree-in-bud nodularity makes primary malignancy less likely.
An infectious pseudotumor-like lesion is more likely than primary malignancy.
The third differential is an anastomotic complication such as granulation tissue or bronchial stenosis.
The location at the anastomosis fits anastomotic complication.
Severe luminal narrowing fits anastomotic complication.
Granulation tissue alone would not as readily explain the constitutional symptom of night sweats.
Granulation tissue alone would not as readily explain hemoptysis.
Granulation tissue alone would not as readily explain tree-in-bud nodularity.
The lesion is described as a fibrinous mass rather than simple scar or granulation tissue.
In an immunocompromised host, infection superimposed on the anastomosis is more likely.
The fourth and most compelling differential is fungal tracheobronchitis or endobronchial fungal infection.
Aspergillus involving the bronchial anastomosis is especially considered.
Lung transplant recipients are particularly susceptible to Aspergillus airway infection at bronchial anastomoses.
Impaired local vascularity contributes to susceptibility to Aspergillus airway infection at bronchial anastomoses.
Impaired healing contributes to susceptibility to Aspergillus airway infection at bronchial anastomoses.

The case features supporting Aspergillus tracheobronchitis are immunosuppression, diabetes, profound leukopenia, a lesion arising at the anastomotic site, bronchoscopic appearance of a fibrinous obstructing mass, hemoptysis, focal wheeze from airway obstruction, and tree-in-bud nodularity distal to the lesion.
Aspergillus tracheobronchitis can present as pseudomembranous endobronchial masses.
Aspergillus tracheobronchitis can present as obstructing endobronchial masses.
Aspergillus tracheobronchitis may present without classic invasive pneumonia.
Fever may be absent in Aspergillus tracheobronchitis.
The single most likely diagnosis is obstructing Aspergillus tracheobronchitis at the bronchial anastomosis after lung transplantation.
This diagnosis best explains the focal endobronchial fibrinous mass.
This diagnosis best explains the severe left mainstem narrowing.
This diagnosis best explains the distal tree-in-bud changes.
This diagnosis best explains the patient’s immunocompromised post-transplant state.
The final diagnosis is Aspergillus tracheobronchitis.
